This provided former students with truth, healing and compensation. Back in the day residential schools weren't talked about at school or anywhere so for this to be implemented and for the truth to finally be out there must be a relief to any survivors out there.","slide_2":"Probably the Health and Healing Services because the survivors were the ones most impacted by these schools and they suffered a crazy amount of physical and mental abuse so for the survivors to be able to get assistance after experiencing all of that is crictical. Yes, getting a direct payment is nice and all, but it doesn't remove what happened in the past and the abuse suffered. No amount of money can justify what happened in those schools.","slide_3":"Shubenacadie Indian Residential School was the only residential school that was located in Nova Scotia. The school opened in 1929 and closed for 1967 so the school operated for 38 years. The church that was responsible for the administration of this school was the Roman Catholic Church.","slide_4":"The (CEP) would give her a payment for having to reside at a recognized residential school. This payment would try and make up for her experience of being at a residential school. The (TRC) would allow her to tell her stories and her experience about the residential schools. It would allow for the truth to be out there and to show just how bad the schools actually were."}

{"slide_1":"The implementation of the IRSSA was a turning point because it saw the government admit, in some way, to the horrors it inflicted on Indigenous children, and saw it make some attempt to reconcile.","slide_2":"Health and Healing Services are the most important as they help people move past trauma and stop cycles of abuse. This benefits survivors, their children, and the community by potentially reducing rates of suicide and drug abuse through proactive support.","slide_3":"Shubenacadie Indian Residential School


• Operational Duration: 38 years


• Administration: Catholic Church","slide_4":"Common Experience Payment (CEP): Betty would receive a standardized payment for her time spent as a residential school survivor.

Independent Assessment Process (IAP): Provided Betty testified to her experiences, this would provide specific compensation for the sexual and physical abuses she suffered.

Proposed Resource Allocation: * Expansion of Indigenous language lessons.

Funding for specialized therapies and medical aids required due to past abuses."}

{"slide_1":"The Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSA) is recognized as a critical turning point in Canadian history. Its significance lies in:

National Recognition: It marked the formal acknowledgment of the systemic harm and trauma inflicted upon children within the residential school system.

The Healing Process: It serves as the foundational starting point for the long-term healing journey of Indigenous peoples, moving toward reconciliation.","slide_2":"Among the various pillars of the settlement, Health and Healing is identified as a primary focus due to the following factors:

Physical Hardship: Survivors were subjected to forced labor and harsh environments.

Psychological Impact: The abusive nature of the schools led to significant mental health challenges, including chronic depression and long-term trauma.

Rehabilitation: Targeted health services are essential to address these specific historical injuries and support the well-being of survivors.","slide_3":"the indian residential school was operational for 37 years and was administrated by a catholic church."}

{"title":"Wolf","description":"I chose the wolf as my final project because the wolf is one of the Grandfathers' seven teachings used to guide us to be the best humans we can be.  The wolf represents community and humility, family values, and leadership. The wolf teaches us to care for others and to give before we take for ourselves. They are very smart hunters. No family member will go hungry or unprotected in the pack.\nThe wolf also shows us good family values. They mate for life and rely on all ages from the young to the elderly for survival. Wolves believe in protecting their family members. \nMy painting also represents the creativity of the Mi’knaw people. We use our own individual ideas to create our art. I chose to show the many different layers in the wolf’s personality by layering the paint to add colors at each level. You can’t see all the levels in the final painting but they are there, just like all the traits of the wolf are always present but only used when the wolf needs to provide or protect it’s family members. I also chose to show the wolf’s strength by placing him above the land below, on a ledge talking to mother earth at night. Mother earth is our knowledge keeper and who we ask and give thanks for every living and non-living thing."}

No family member will go hungry or unprotected in the pack.\nThe wolf also shows us good family values. They mate for life and rely on all ages from the young to the elderly for survival. Wolves believe in protecting their family members. \nMy painting also represents the creativity of the Mi’knaw people. We use our own individual ideas to create our art. I chose to show the many different layers in the wolf’s personality by layering the paint to add colors at each level. You can’t see all the levels in the final painting but they are there, just like all the traits of the wolf are always present but only used when the wolf needs to provide or protect it’s family members. I also chose to show the wolf’s strength by placing him above the land below, on a ledge talking to mother earth at night. Mother earth is our knowledge keeper and who we ask and give thanks for every living and non-living thing."}
